title: Tenant rate limits and usage invoices
scenario: A month of API events is replayed through a per-tenant sliding-minute limiter (overrides, suspension via override 0, unlimited enterprise), then allowed units are invoiced with included units, round-up overage and credits. Test 3 is the finance statement.

verified.why_correct: Treating an all-digit string as epoch seconds and calling fromtimestamp looks like a timezone trap, but it passes tz=timezone.utc, and the two text formats get tzinfo=UTC too, so every timestamp is aware UTC and they compare and subtract consistently (1777633210 is 2026-05-01 11:00:10 UTC).

bugs.title: Enterprise check compares the Plan enum to a string
bugs.symptom: test_1_limits.test_enterprise_not_throttled: orbit has ['2026-05-01 14:00:40', '2026-05-01 14:00:50'] throttled instead of []. Its invoice is unchanged (flat enterprise fee).
bugs.why: tenant.plan is a Plan member, and a plain Enum member never equals its value string ('enterprise'), so the enterprise branch never runs and orbit falls through to the plan's advisory rpm of 4.
hints: orbit is enterprise, so why is it throttled at all?
Check what type tenant.plan is when limit_for compares it.
Compare enum to enum: tenant.plan is Plan.ENTERPRISE (drop .value).
probes: Would this comparison have worked if Plan subclassed str?
Why didn't orbit's invoice change even though two requests were throttled?

bugs.title: Request exactly 60 s old still counted in the window
bugs.symptom: test_1_limits.test_window_boundary: kestrel's throttled list is ['2026-05-01 10:01:00'] instead of ['2026-05-01 10:01:05'].
bugs.why: The window is (ts - 60s, ts], so a request exactly 60 s earlier must be evicted. With `>` it stays, kestrel's 10:01:00 request sees 3 in the window and is throttled; that frees a slot, so 10:01:05 is allowed instead.
hints: kestrel's throttled time is 10:01:00. How far is that from its first request?
Look at the eviction condition in apply_limit.
Evict when the age is >= WINDOW_S.
probes: Why did the 10:01:05 request flip from throttled to allowed?

bugs.title: rpm_override 0 collapsed to None
bugs.symptom: test_1_limits.test_suspended_tenant: ivory's throttled list is [] instead of all three of its requests.
bugs.why: `or None` turns the real override 0 into 'no override', so suspended ivory is treated as an ordinary enterprise tenant with no limit.
hints: ivory should be suspended. What does tenants.csv say, and what does the Tenant object hold?
Follow rpm_override from the CSV into limit_for.
Drop the `or None`; parse_int already returns None for blank.
probes: Why does limit_for test `is not None` rather than truthiness?

bugs.why: credits.json has ' Delta-Labs '. clean() strips it to 'Delta-Labs', which doesn't match the tenant id 'delta-labs', so credits.get falls back to 0.
hints: delta-labs has a credit in credits.json. Why is credit_cents 0?
Compare how tenant ids and credit keys are normalised.
Use norm_id(k) for the credit keys.

Where else could a silent .get(..., 0) fallback hide a lookup mismatch?

bugs.title: Overage part-cents floored instead of rounded up
bugs.symptom: test_2_invoices.test_overage_part_cents: harbor shows gross_cents 3200 and amount_cents 3000 (expected 3201 / 3001).
bugs.why: harbor's overage is 1203 units x 250 / 1000 = 300.75 cents. Floor division gives 300, but the spec rounds part-cents up to 301. The double negation is how the reference gets a ceiling from //.
hints: harbor is one cent short. Work its overage out by hand.
Look at how overage_cents turns a fractional cent into an integer.
probes: Why did delta-labs come out right?
Why does -(-a // b) give a ceiling?

bugs.title: Top tenants sorted quietest first
bugs.why: Without the minus the sort is ascending by request count, so the slice takes the three quietest tenants, despite the 'busiest first' comment.
hints: top_tenants lists quill with 1 request. Does that match 'most requests first'?
Look at the sort key for top.
Negate the count: key=lambda t: (-requests[t], t).
probes: Why not just add reverse=True to the original key?
Why does nimbus never appear here, even though it sent requests?

context_qa.q: What does build_report do, in order?
context_qa.a: Loads plans, tenants, credits and events (events only for known active tenants), groups events by tenant, then for each active tenant (sorted) calls apply_limit with limit_for's result and builds an invoice from the allowed events. The statement is built from all loaded events and the invoices.
The tenant's rpm_override if it isn't None; otherwise None for the plan checked in its second `if`; otherwise plans[tenant.plan].rpm. None means apply_limit allows everything.

context_qa.q: How does apply_limit maintain its window?
context_qa.a: It sorts the tenant's events by ts and keeps a deque of timestamps of allowed requests. Before each event it pops timestamps from the left while the condition in its while-loop holds, then allows the event if limit is None or the deque is shorter than limit. Only allowed requests are appended.

context_qa.q: What type is Tenant.plan and how is it parsed?
context_qa.a: It is a `Plan` member (a plain `Enum` with values 'free', 'pro', 'enterprise'), built with `Plan(norm_id(row['plan']))` in load_tenants. Invoices output `tenant.plan.value`.
`parse_ts` treats an all-digit string as epoch seconds via fromtimestamp(..., tz=UTC), otherwise tries '%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ' then '%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S' and attaches UTC.

context_qa.q: How is a tenant's credit looked up?
context_qa.a: load_credits builds a dict from credits.json, transforming each key in its comprehension; build_report then calls credits.get(tenant_id, 0) with the normalised tenant id.

A Counter of tenant_id over every loaded event, so allowed and throttled requests both count, but ignored events (unknown or inactive tenants) don't. It is sorted with a key over the count and tenant id and sliced to TOP_N = 3.
